tagline: The first half of a two-volume history: the story of Jesus, Savior of the poor, the outsider, and the lost, told to a man named Theophilus so that he might know the certainty of what he had been taught.
overview:
Luke is the longest of the four Gospels and the first of two books by the same author; the second is the Acts of the Apostles. It opens with something none of the other Gospels has, a formal preface in polished Greek that explains the author's method: many have written accounts, the material was handed down by eyewitnesses, and he has investigated everything carefully in order to write an orderly account for “most excellent Theophilus” (1:3). Then the story begins in the temple in Jerusalem, with an old priest and a promise, and moves through the births of John the Baptist and Jesus, Jesus' ministry in Galilee, a long section on the road to Jerusalem, and his death, resurrection, and ascension.

Much of Luke's material appears in no other Gospel. Only Luke tells of the shepherds at the manger, the boy Jesus in the temple, the Good Samaritan, the lost coin and the lost son, the rich man and Lazarus, Zacchaeus in the tree, the thief on the cross who is promised paradise, and the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. These stories share a direction. The good news comes to the poor, the sick, women, Samaritans, tax collectors, and sinners, and it comes with joy. Jesus sums up his own mission near the end: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10).

Luke matters because it shows the story of Jesus as history that fulfills Israel's Scriptures and opens toward the whole world. It begins among faithful Jews waiting in the temple for the consolation of Israel and ends with the risen Jesus explaining that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled (24:44), and that repentance and forgiveness will be preached to all nations. Acts then tells how that happened.
author:
The Gospel does not name its author, but the tradition that it was written by Luke is early and uniform. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon near the end of the second century, names Luke as the author and calls him a follower of Paul, and the Muratorian fragment, an early list of accepted books usually dated to the late second century, says the same. No other name was ever attached to the book.

Luke appears three times in Paul's letters. Colossians 4:14 sends greetings from “Luke, the beloved physician,” Philemon 24 lists him among Paul's fellow workers, and 2 Timothy 4:11 says “Only Luke is with me.” In Colossians Paul appears to list Luke separately from the coworkers who are Jewish (4:10-11), which is why many conclude Luke was a Gentile, though some dispute that reading. The strongest internal evidence comes from Acts. In several sections the narrative shifts without explanation from “they” to “we” (16:10-17, 20:5-21:18, and 27:1-28:16), placing the writer at Paul's side in Philippi, on the voyage to Jerusalem, and on the ship to Rome. The traditional reading is that the author was present for those events, and Luke is the companion who best fits. Some scholars think the we sections come from a travel diary the author used, perhaps his own, and a few have argued that the first person is a literary device found in ancient sea-voyage stories; critics of that view reply that no clear parallel explains an author slipping into the first person without comment.

The older argument that the book's medical vocabulary proves a physician wrote it (made in the nineteenth century by W. K. Hobart) was weakened when Henry Cadbury showed that educated writers without medical training used much the same vocabulary. The claim now rests on the tradition and on Acts, not on the vocabulary. Whoever the author was, he wrote the most literary Greek in the Gospels, knew the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, the translation used by Greek-speaking Jews) intimately, and wrote as a historian of the early church.
date: The date depends partly on Acts, since Luke's Gospel was written before it (Acts 1:1 refers back to the first book). Three main positions are held. Some date both books to the early 60s AD, noting that Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years (around AD 60 to 62) and says nothing of his death, the persecution under Nero, or the fall of Jerusalem. Most scholars date the Gospel between about AD 75 and 90, arguing that Luke used Mark, which is usually dated to the late 60s or around 70, and that Luke's wording of Jesus' prophecy, “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies” (21:20), reflects the Roman siege of AD 70. Those who hold the earlier date answer that Jesus' prophecy draws on Old Testament language about sieges and need not have been written after the event, and that Acts may end where it does because Paul had reached Rome, the goal of the story. A minority, notably Richard Pervo, places Acts in the early second century. On any view the book was written within the lifetime of people who had known the eyewitnesses or their hearers.
setting:
The story is set in Judea and Galilee under Roman rule, from the last years of Herod the Great (who died in 4 BC) to the governorship of Pontius Pilate (about AD 26 to 36). Luke anchors it in public history more carefully than any other Gospel writer. The birth is dated by the emperor Augustus and a census under Quirinius, governor of Syria (2:1-2), and John's preaching by the fifteenth year of Tiberius, with Pilate governing Judea, Herod Antipas ruling Galilee, and Annas and Caiaphas holding the high priesthood (3:1-2). The Jerusalem temple, rebuilt on a grand scale by Herod the Great, frames the book: it opens with Zechariah burning incense there and closes with the disciples praising God in its courts (24:53).

The first readers are harder to place. Theophilus has a Greek name meaning friend of God, and the title “most excellent” was used for men of rank, such as Roman governors in Acts. He may have been a patron who paid for the book's copying and circulation, a common practice for ancient authors, or a believer of standing who had been instructed in the faith. Beyond him the book seems written for a mainly Gentile church that wanted to know how a movement born among Jews in Judea came to include people like them, and whether it could be trusted.
purpose: Luke states his purpose himself: he has written so that Theophilus may know the certainty of the things he has been taught (1:4). The book is meant to confirm faith by setting out what happened in order, grounded in eyewitness testimony. It also answers questions a Gentile church faced near the end of the first century. Was this a legitimate continuation of Israel's faith, or a new sect? Luke shows that Jesus fulfills God's promises to Israel and that the inclusion of Gentiles was part of God's plan from the start. Was it a threat to Roman order? Luke notes repeatedly that Roman officials found no fault in Jesus (23:4, 23:14-15, 23:22) and, in Acts, in Paul. And who belongs in this community? Luke's answer is that the poor, the sinful, and the outsider are welcomed, and that the rich and the respectable are called to repentance with everyone else.
story: Luke picks up the Old Testament story where it paused. Its first chapters are full of the language of the Greek Old Testament: an old childless couple like Abraham and Sarah or Elkanah and Hannah, the angel Gabriel from Daniel, and songs that echo Hannah's prayer and the Psalms. The long silence after the prophets ends with John, who comes in the spirit and power of Elijah, as Malachi had promised. The Gospel then tells how God's promise to David and to Abraham is kept in Jesus. It ends where Acts begins, with the ascension and the command to wait in Jerusalem for power from on high. Acts carries the same story from Jerusalem to Rome, so that the two books together cover the arc from the temple in Jerusalem to the capital of the Gentile world.
christ: Luke presents Jesus as Savior, a title the angels announce to shepherds (2:11) and one Luke uses more than Matthew or Mark. He is the Son of David who will reign forever, the Son of God conceived by the Holy Spirit, and the prophet anointed by the Spirit to preach good news to the poor. In his first sermon at Nazareth he reads from Isaiah 61, “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor” (4:18), and says the Scripture is fulfilled that day. Luke also stresses that his suffering was necessary: the risen Jesus explains to the Emmaus disciples, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, what was written in all the Scriptures about himself (24:27). The church confesses on this ground that Jesus is truly God and truly man, crucified for sinners, bodily raised (Luke insists he eats fish before the disciples, 24:42-43), and ascended to the Father.
reading:
Read Luke as an ancient history written by a believer, not as a modern biography. Luke selects and arranges his material, sometimes by theme rather than strict chronology, and he often pairs stories of a man and a woman (Simeon and Anna, the shepherd with his sheep and the woman with her coin). Notice his many parables, most of them unique to him, and pay attention to who is eating with whom; meals are one of the book's main settings. The long central section (9:51-19:27) is framed as Jesus' road to Jerusalem, but it is less a travel log than a collection of teaching on discipleship, wealth, prayer, and the kingdom gathered under that heading.

Luke also needs to be read with Acts. Themes that begin in the Gospel, such as the Spirit, prayer, witnesses, and the gospel going out to the nations, come to full expression in the second volume. Readers comparing Luke with Matthew and Mark will see that the three share much material; most scholars think Luke used Mark and a second source shared with Matthew (often called Q, from the German Quelle, source), while others argue that Luke knew Matthew directly. Luke himself says he drew on earlier written accounts and eyewitness testimony (1:1-2), which fits either view.

structure.title: Preface to Theophilus
structure.summary: Luke explains that he has investigated everything from the eyewitnesses and written an orderly account so that Theophilus may know the certainty of what he was taught.

structure.title: The births of John and Jesus
structure.summary: Angelic announcements, the songs of Mary, Zechariah, and Simeon, the birth in Bethlehem, and the boy Jesus in the temple show God keeping his promises to Israel.

structure.title: Preparation for ministry
structure.summary: John preaches repentance, Jesus is baptized and anointed by the Spirit, his genealogy is traced back to Adam, and he is tested in the wilderness.

structure.title: Ministry in Galilee
structure.summary: Jesus announces good news to the poor at Nazareth, heals, forgives, calls disciples, teaches, and is confessed by Peter as the Christ of God before foretelling his suffering.

structure.title: The road to Jerusalem
structure.summary: Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem and teaches on discipleship, prayer, wealth, and the kingdom, including many parables found only in Luke, such as the Good Samaritan and the lost son.

structure.title: Teaching in Jerusalem
structure.summary: Jesus enters the city, weeps over it, clears the temple, answers his opponents, and foretells Jerusalem's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man.

structure.title: The passion
structure.summary: Jesus shares the Passover meal, prays on the Mount of Olives, is betrayed, tried before the council, Pilate, and Herod, crucified between two criminals, and buried.

structure.title: Resurrection and ascension
structure.summary: The women find the tomb empty, the risen Jesus meets disciples on the Emmaus road and in Jerusalem, opens the Scriptures to them, and is taken up into heaven.

themes.title: Good news to the poor
themes.body: Luke gives more attention to wealth and poverty than any other Gospel. Mary sings that God has filled the hungry and sent the rich away empty (1:53), Jesus' first sermon announces good news to the poor (4:18), his beatitudes bless the poor and pronounce woes on the rich (6:20-26), and parables like the rich fool and the rich man and Lazarus warn against trusting in possessions. Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector who gives away half his goods, shows what repentance can look like with money.

themes.title: Women and outsiders
themes.body: Women are prominent throughout Luke: Elizabeth, Mary, and Anna in the birth stories, the women who supported Jesus from their own means (8:1-3), Mary of Bethany sitting at his feet as a disciple, and the women who witness the cross and first hear of the resurrection. Samaritans, whom many Jews despised, appear as the neighbor in the parable and the one grateful leper among ten. Tax collectors and sinners are welcomed at Jesus' table, which scandalizes his critics.

themes.title: Prayer
themes.body: Luke shows Jesus praying at the turning points of his life: at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, before Peter's confession, at the transfiguration, in Gethsemane, and on the cross. Only Luke records the parables of the persistent friend at midnight, the persistent widow, and the Pharisee and the tax collector praying in the temple. Prayer in Luke is the ordinary posture of those who wait on God.

themes.title: The Holy Spirit
themes.body: The Spirit is active from the first chapter: John is filled with the Spirit from the womb, Mary conceives by the Spirit's power, and Elizabeth, Zechariah, and Simeon speak by the Spirit. Jesus is anointed by the Spirit at his baptism and returns to Galilee in the Spirit's power. At the end he promises the disciples power from on high, which comes at Pentecost in Acts 2.

themes.title: Salvation today, and joy
themes.body: The word today carries weight in Luke: today a Savior is born (2:11), today the Scripture is fulfilled (4:21), today salvation has come to Zacchaeus's house (19:9), today the thief will be with Jesus in paradise (23:43). Salvation is present, not only future. And it brings joy: the angels announce good news of great joy, and heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents (15:7).

keyChapters.why: The preface explains Luke's method, and the announcements to Zechariah and Mary, with Mary's song, set out the book's themes of reversal and fulfillment.
The birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, the shepherds, and Simeon's words about a light for the Gentiles anchor the good news in history and point to its reach.
Jesus' sermon at Nazareth from Isaiah 61 is his program statement for the whole ministry, and his rejection there foreshadows what follows.
The parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son show God's joy in finding the lost and expose the resentment of those who think they were never lost.
Zacchaeus's conversion and Jesus' statement that he came to seek and to save the lost lead into his entry into Jerusalem.
The empty tomb, the Emmaus road, and the ascension show the risen Jesus opening the Scriptures and sending his disciples to the nations.
